title: How QM switches agent vendors mid-conversation without losing history
summary: QM is a self-hosted 'multiplayer agent harness' that gives every employee an isolated agent workspace on Slack and the web — and lets an org swap Pi, Codex, or Claude Code under the same sessions.
body_html:
What it is

QM, from yc-software, calls itself a "multiplayer agent harness for work," and the phrase is doing real work. Most agent products are personal assistants: one user, one memory, one set of credentials. Stretch that across a company and you get a single shared brain that everyone is simultaneously reconfiguring. QM's answer is scopes. Each person and each room — a Slack channel, a group message, a project — gets its own memory, files, keychain view, permissions, cron jobs, and a durable sandbox where installed tools stay installed. The same identity carries between Slack and a web app, so the agent you tuned in a DM is the one you meet in the browser.

Two weeks after its first commit it sits at ~13k stars, and the trending appeal is easy to read: it's an open-source, self-hostable take on the "company agent" that several vendors sell as SaaS — with the unusual twist that it isn't married to any one AI vendor. Pi, OpenCode, Codex, and Claude Code all drive the same core, chosen by org config.

How it actually works

The architecture is a headless TypeScript core (Node + Fastify) with everything user-facing bolted on as plugins: the web UI (Vite + Lit), the admin panel, the public portal, and a Slack plugin built on Bolt that the core starts and supervises in-process. Postgres holds sessions, memory, and the work queue. The agent itself has a deliberately small, fixed tool surface; one of those tools is execute, which runs commands inside the scope's own isolated sandbox rather than on the host.

Everything specific to one company — org config, custom tools and skills, the sandbox image, infrastructure — lives outside the core in a "deployment directory" that the qm CLI validates and deploys to your own Fly or AWS account. Every substrate (harness, session store, sandbox, memory) sits behind an interface and gets wired up in a single file, which is what makes the vendor-swapping possible.

The interesting detail: sessions outlive the harness

The part worth reading closely is src/harness/harness-router.ts. QM treats a vendor harness as a disposable adapter, not the owner of the conversation. Session history lives in QM's Postgres store and is passed into every turn; whatever session state Codex or Claude Code keeps on its side is just a cache. That makes mid-conversation vendor switching almost boringly simple:

async runTurn(input) {
  const choice = await resolve(input);
  const adapter = adapters.get(choice.harnessId);
  if (!adapter) throw new Error(`harness ${choice.harnessId} is unavailable`);
  const prior = lastHarness.get(input.session.id);
  if (prior && prior !== choice.harnessId) {
    await adapters.get(prior)?.turns.resetSession?.(input.session.id);
    await adapter.turns.resetSession?.(input.session.id);
  }
  lastHarness.set(input.session.id, choice.harnessId);
  return adapter.turns.runTurn({ ...input, harness: choice.harnessId, model: choice.modelId });
}

If the resolved harness differs from the one that served the last turn, the router resets both vendors' provider-side sessions and re-runs the turn — the new adapter rebuilds its context from the core-owned history. Each adapter also declares a profile (control transport, tool transport, capabilities like steer or abort), so the core knows what it can ask of each vendor without importing any vendor SDK directly.

The security model is similarly opinionated: an org picks one posture that narrower scopes can only tighten. Strict pauses every tool call for human approval; Auto (the default) runs a classifier over provenance-labelled external content before the model sees it — a prompt-injection screen; Dangerous drops both, but a predeclared command policy (hard denials for recursive deletes, destructive SQL) applies in every posture.

Who should use it

  • Startups that want one agent deployment where each employee gets an isolated, customizable workspace plus shared project channels.
  • Teams hedging vendor risk: harness and model are org config, and switching doesn't strand your session data.
  • Operators who want the whole thing in their own cloud account, with an audit trail.

Two caveats before you deploy. First, the agent acts with the user's real credentials and permissions — QM's own SECURITY.md is upfront that this follows the local-coding-agent trust model, audited rather than sandboxed away. Second, the contribution policy is unusual: the maintainers accept descriptions of changes as text files, not code PRs — they implement everything themselves. If you need to customize beyond the deployment directory, the README walks through maintaining a private mirror-clone (deliberately not a GitHub fork, which can't be made private) that tracks upstream.
